title: How to pay international contractors (2026 guide) | Ontop
summary: Compare 5 ways to pay international contractors, from wires to a contractor payment platform. Costs, speed, FX and the IRS rules for 2026.
body_markdown:
*Updated October 2026*


**The short answer:** there are five ways to pay international contractors. You can send an international bank wire, use a payment platform or multi-currency account, pay through local payout rails, pay in stablecoins such as USDC, or use a contractor of record that contracts and pays the contractor for you. Wires are simple but slow and expensive at scale. Platforms move money but leave contracts, tax forms and classification on your desk. A contractor of record handles payments and compliance in one place, which is why it is the default for companies paying more than a handful of people abroad.


For a US company, the tax side is shorter than most people expect. Collect a Form W-8BEN from each non-US contractor, keep it on file, and you generally do not issue a Form 1099-NEC for work performed outside the US. The real risk is not the IRS paperwork. It is misclassification under the contractor's local labor law.


## Key takeaways


- Five payment methods cover almost every case: bank wire (SWIFT), payment platforms, local payouts, stablecoins and contractor of record.
- Speed and cost depend more on the corridor and the FX margin than on the headline fee.
- Non-US contractors give you a Form W-8BEN, not a W-9. Work done fully outside the US is generally foreign-source income, so no 1099-NEC and no US withholding ([IRS Publication 515](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p515) ).
- Payment tools move money. They do not make someone a contractor. Classification is decided by how the work actually happens.
- Small teams and agencies get the most from consolidating: one contract flow, one payout run, one set of records.


## The 5 ways to pay international contractors, compared


Here is how the methods compare on what actually changes your monthly cost and your risk. Speeds and fees vary by country, currency and provider, so treat this as a starting map, not a quote.


Method Speed Cost FX Compliance burden on you


**International bank wire (SWIFT)** Usually a few business days, varies by corridor Sending fee per wire, plus possible intermediary bank deductions Bank rate, often with a markup High: contracts, tax forms and records are all yours


**Payment platform or multi-currency account** Often faster than a wire, varies by provider Per-transfer or percentage fee Varies: some show the margin, some hide it in the rate Medium to high: payments only, classification stays with you


**Local payouts** (ACH, SEPA, PIX, SPEI and similar rails) Fast where a local rail exists Low per payout once set up Depends on who converts and when Medium: needs a provider with local accounts in each country


**Stablecoins** (USDC) Minutes on-chain; cashing out to a local bank varies Network fee plus off-ramp fee Contractor keeps USD value and converts later Medium to high: local crypto rules and tax records differ by country


**Contractor of record** Scheduled payout runs set by the provider Monthly fee per contractor (Ontop from $49) Handled by the provider, contractor chooses how to receive Low: the provider contracts the contractor, carries classification responsibility and keeps the records


## 1. International bank wire (SWIFT)


A wire is the oldest way to pay someone abroad. You send money from your business bank account through the SWIFT network, and it may pass through one or more correspondent banks before it reaches the contractor's bank.


### Best for


One or two contractors, large and infrequent invoices, or countries where the contractor only has a traditional bank account.


### What to watch


Intermediary banks can deduct fees on the way, so the contractor may receive less than you sent. The exchange rate your bank applies usually carries a margin you do not see on the invoice. Every wire also needs its own reconciliation, which adds up once you pay ten people every month.


## 2. Payment platforms and multi-currency accounts


Online payment platforms and multi-currency accounts let you pay contractors from a dashboard, often at a better rate than a bank. This is what most people mean when they search for a **contractor payment platform** .


### Best for


Teams that already have contracts and tax documents handled and just need a cheaper, faster way to move money.


### What to watch


Most platforms are payment rails, not compliance tools. They will not draft a compliant contract for each country, check classification, or keep the records an auditor will ask for. Compare the full cost: transfer fee, FX margin, and any fee charged to the contractor on receipt.


## 3. Local payouts


With local payouts, the provider holds accounts inside each country and pays the contractor over domestic rails, such as SEPA in Europe, PIX in Brazil or SPEI in Mexico. For the contractor it looks like a local transfer.


### Best for


Recurring payments to several contractors in the same countries, where speed and predictable arrival dates matter.


### What to watch


Coverage is uneven. Check that the provider supports every country you pay today and the ones you plan to hire in next.


## 4. Stablecoins (USDC)


Some contractors, especially in countries with volatile local currencies, prefer to be paid in a dollar-backed stablecoin like USDC. Payment settles on-chain in minutes, and the contractor decides when to convert.


### Best for


Contractors who want to hold dollars and already know how to cash out safely in their country.


### What to watch


Rules for crypto assets differ by country, and you still need the same contract, tax form and payment record as with any other method. Offer it as a choice, not as the only option.


## 5. Contractor of record


A contractor of record engages the contractor on your behalf under a compliant agreement, takes on the classification responsibility, and pays them. You approve the work and fund one payout run. The provider handles the contracts, documents and payments across countries.


It is not an employer of record. Nobody becomes an employee, so there is no local payroll, no benefits package and no EOR price tag. Most global teams start with contractors, and for them a contractor of record is the lighter, cheaper path. Read more about[how a contractor of record works](https://www.getontop.com/blog/contractor-of-record) and why it is often the[EOR alternative for contractor teams](https://www.getontop.com/solutions/eor-alternative-for-contractors) .


### Best for


Companies paying contractors in several countries that want one contract flow, one payout run and one place for compliance records.


### What to watch


Check the price per contractor, the countries covered, how payouts reach the contractor, and what the provider is actually responsible for in writing.


## How to pay an international contractor, step by step


1. **Confirm it is a contractor relationship.** If you set the hours, supply the tools and manage the work like an employee's, it may not be one. See the classification section below.
2. **Sign a written agreement.** Define scope, rates, currency, payment terms, IP ownership and termination. Start from an[independent contractor agreement](https://www.getontop.com/blog/independent-contractor-agreement) and adapt it to the country.
3. **Collect the right tax form.** Form W-8BEN for non-US individuals, Form W-9 for US persons living abroad.
4. **Agree on currency and payout method.** USD or local currency, and which of the five methods above.
5. **Get an invoice for each payment.** It is your record of what was paid and why.
6. **Pay and reconcile.** Match each payment to its invoice and keep the confirmation.
7. **Keep the file.** Contract, tax form, invoices and payment records, per contractor.


## US tax and compliance rules when you pay contractors abroad


This section covers the US side for US-based companies. It is general information, not tax advice, and the contractor's own country has its own rules.


### Form W-8BEN for non-US contractors


Ask every non-US individual contractor for a Form W-8BEN. It certifies they are a foreign person. You keep it in your records; it is not sent to the IRS ([IRS, About Form W-8 BEN](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-w-8-ben) ;[Instructions for Form W-8BEN](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/iw8ben) ). Foreign companies use Form W-8BEN-E instead.


### No 1099-NEC for work done outside the US


Pay for services performed outside the US by a nonresident is generally foreign-source income. It is not subject to US withholding and you generally do not report it on Form 1099-NEC ([IRS Publication 515](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p515) ;[Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) ). Two exceptions matter. A US citizen or resident living abroad is still a US person: collect a W-9 and issue a 1099-NEC. And if a foreign contractor does part of the work while physically in the US, that part can be US-source income subject to withholding and reporting on[Form 1042-S](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-1042-s) . More detail in[do foreign contractors pay US taxes](https://www.getontop.com/blog/do-foreign-contractors-pay-us-taxes) .


### Misclassification is the real risk


The IRS looks at behavioral control, financial control and the relationship of the parties to decide whether someone is an independent contractor ([IRS, Independent contractor or employee](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/independent-contractor-self-employed-or-employee) ). Abroad, the stricter test is usually the contractor's local labor law. A long, exclusive, full-time arrangement with set hours can be treated as employment, with back pay, benefits and penalties attached. See the[most common misclassification risks](https://www.getontop.com/blog/contractor-misclassification-risks) .


### Sanctions screening


US companies cannot pay people or entities on US sanctions lists. Screen new contractors before the first payment ([OFAC Sanctions List Service](https://ofac.treasury.gov/sanctions-list-service) ). Most regulated payment providers do this as part of onboarding.


## How to choose a contractor payment platform


Whatever you pick, ask these questions before you move the first contractor:


- **Total cost per payment:** transfer fee, FX margin and anything the contractor pays to receive.
- **Coverage:** every country you pay today, and the next three you plan to hire in.
- **Payout choice:** local bank, USD account, card or stablecoin, chosen by the contractor.
- **Compliance scope:** does it only move money, or does it also handle contracts, tax forms and classification?
- **Records:** can you export contracts, invoices and payment history for your accountant in one go?
- **Support:** who answers when a payment is held, and how fast?


## If you're a small business or agency


Many companies paying international contractors are small teams. A five-person agency with designers in Colombia and developers in Argentina has the same compliance questions as a large company, with no finance team to answer them.


### Start simple, then consolidate


With one or two contractors, a wire or a payment platform plus a solid contract and a W-8BEN on file is enough. Once you pass three or four people, or pay in more than one country, the hours spent on invoices, reconciliation and contracts usually cost more than a per-contractor fee. That is the point to move everyone to one system.


### Agencies paying for client work


If you resell contractor work to clients, keep the contract chain clean: your agreement with the contractor, your agreement with the client, and records that tie each payment to a project. It makes invoicing and audits much easier.

## FAQ


### What is the best way to pay international contractors?


For one or two contractors, a payment platform with a clear FX margin is usually enough. For several contractors in different countries, a contractor of record is the best way, because it covers contracts, classification and payments in one flow.


### How do I pay an international contractor as a US company?


Sign a written agreement, collect a Form W-8BEN, agree on currency and method, get an invoice, then pay by wire, payment platform, local payout, stablecoin or through a contractor of record. Keep the contract, form, invoices and payment records on file.


### Do I need to send a 1099 to a foreign contractor?


Generally no. A nonresident who performs all the work outside the US gives you a W-8BEN instead, and that income is not reported on Form 1099-NEC. US citizens living abroad are the exception: they still get a 1099-NEC.


### What is a contractor payment platform?


Software that lets a company pay independent contractors, often across borders and currencies, from one dashboard. Some only move money. Others, like a contractor of record, also handle contracts, tax documents and compliance.


### Is a contractor of record the same as an employer of record?


No. An employer of record hires people as employees, with local payroll and benefits. A contractor of record keeps people as independent contractors and handles their contracts, compliance and payments, at a much lower cost.


### How long do international contractor payments take?


It depends on the method and the corridor. Wires usually take a few business days, local payouts are faster where a local rail exists, and stablecoins settle in minutes on-chain. With Ontop, most payouts land in the contractor's[Ontop Global Account](https://www.getontop.com/ontop-global-account) in about 15 minutes; withdrawals to a local bank then follow local rails.


### Can I pay international contractors in USD?


Yes. Many contractors prefer USD to protect their income from local currency swings. You can pay in USD by wire, through a USD account, in a dollar-backed stablecoin, or through a contractor of record that lets each contractor choose.
